The goal of this benchmark is to provide a tool to get the basic performance overhead of the OpenTelemetry SDK for given events throughput on the target ## Benchmark Configuration ### Span Configuration * No parent `Span` or parent `SpanContext`. * Associated to a resource with attributes `service.name`, `service.version` and 10 characters string value for each attribute, and attribute `` with a unique UUID. * Each `Span` is created and immediately ended. ### Measurement Configuration For the languages with bootstrap cost like JIT compilation, a warm-up phase is recommended to take place before the measurement, which runs under the same ## Throughput Measurement ### Create Spans Number of spans which could be created and exported via OTLP exporter in 1 second per logical core and average number over all logical cores, with each span containing 10 attributes, and each attribute containing two 20 characters strings, one as attribute name the other as value. ## Instrumentation Cost ### CPU Usage Measurement With given number of span throughput specified by user, or 10,000 spans per second as default if user does not input the number, measure and report the CPU usage for SDK with both default configured simple and batching span processors The benchmark should create an out-of-process OTLP receiver which listens on the exporting target or adopts existing OTLP exporter which runs out-of-process, responds with success status immediately and drops The collector should not add significant CPU overhead to the Because the benchmark does not include user processing logic, the total CPU consumption of benchmark program could be considered as approximation of SDK’s CPU consumption. results.title: Performance Overhead
results.content: # Performance Overhead. ## Learn more about how enabling Insights and Tracing in Sentry impacts the performance of your application. Enabling insights and tracing in Sentry SDKs adds some overhead, but should have minimal impact on the performance of your application. They work by instrumenting important parts of typical applications such as:. To perform this instrumentation, Sentry SDKs wrap or monkeypatch specific functions within popular libraries or frameworks and measure the execution time of these operations. The SDKs also make sure to propagate some headers on outgoing requests so that Distributed Tracing can work effectively. For most applications, the performance overhead of enabling insights and tracing in production is imperceptible to end users. ## Will Performance break my application? Each SDK has limits on the data structures used to record all the above data. If your application is doing too many things, we will simply hit those limits and thus avoid scenarios where the SDK itself takes up too much CPU time or grows memory usage unboundedly. We will also capture Outcomes (statistics) whenever these scenarios occur to be transparent about what events we are dropping for what reason. ### Backpressure Management. Some of our backend SDKs manage backpressure internally by reducing the dynamic sampling rate when the system is in an unhealthy state. This ensures better system stability and lower SDK overhead under heavy load. The latest versions of the following SDKs support backpressure management:. Some hosting environments have mechanisms in place that negatively influence SDK overhead:. This means that the SDKs generally will block the response from being finished until it has flushed all of the recorded telemetry data to Sentry. This might cause non-trivial overhead in some situations. Here, it might be beneficial to run a Sentry Relay instance physically close to your lambdas to decrease latency. * SDKs that are designed to run on the Vercel Edge Runtime will stall responses to requests until the SDK has flushed all of the telemetry for that request to Sentry. This is a limitation imposed by the Edge Runtime, since it doesn't allow for I/O operations to be shared or persisted across request handler invocations, meaning the SDK cannot flush its data asynchronously.

Would be great if the runner provide the default request and limit resources for jobs and services, and the user could set custom resource requests and limits for their jobs and services in their `.gitlab-ci.yml`. results.title: How to Handle Backpressure in Streaming
results.content: Backpressure is a common challenge in distributed systems that handle streaming data, such as logs, events, or messages. Managing backpressure in distributed systems is essential for maintaining stability and preventing data loss. Key strategies include: Controlling the Producer: Implement rate limiting to align data generation with processing capacity. Handling backpressure in streaming is crucial for maintaining system stability and performance when dealing with data streams. Here are some common strategies and approaches to manage backpressure effectively: Buffering Flow Control Throttling Reactive Programming Asynchronous Processing Error Handling and Retries Dynamic Scaling Rate Limiting Prioritization Feedback Mechanisms System Monitoring Each strategy or combination of strategies can be applied based on the specific requirements and characteristics of your streaming system. Here's a list of reasons for backpressure in streaming: - slow consumer - high network latency - low buffering capacity - limited resources for the consumer - potential throttling by the consumer client - inefficient error handling by the client. Backpressure in streaming systems occurs when the rate of incoming messages exceeds the system's capacity to process them, leading to a buildup of unprocessed messages. Common indicators of backpressure include increasing queue or buffer size, increasing processing or output time, decreasing throughput, increasing latency, and memory or CPU usage. Preventing or mitigating backpressure in streaming requires adjusting the rate of production and consumption of data, as well as optimizing the processing of data. Strategies mentioned below can proactively minimize the impact of backpressure in any streaming application - focus on optimizing the processing logic at the consumer end (parallelization, resource allocation, etc.) can improve consumer efficiency - implement rate limiting or adaptive throttling techniques which dynamically adjusts the producers rate based on backpressure signals from the consumer - utilize in-memory buffers to temporarily store incoming data and offloading high volume data to disk when the consumer is overloaded (this can introduce additional latency) - consider data sampling to reduce the vol. When determining the best strategy for dealing with backpressure in streaming, it is important to consider the characteristics of your data source and destination, the semantics of your data processing , the trade-offs between throughput and latency, and the cost of your system.

results.title: Performance Overhead - Sentry Docs
results.content: # Performance Overhead ## Learn more about how enabling Insights and Tracing in Sentry impacts the performance of your application. Enabling insights and tracing in Sentry SDKs adds some overhead, but should have minimal impact on the performance of your application. They work by instrumenting important parts of typical applications such as: * Incoming and outgoing HTTP requests * Browser page loads and navigations * Component lifecycle in UI frameworks To perform this instrumentation, Sentry SDKs wrap or monkeypatch specific functions within popular libraries or frameworks and measure the execution time of these operations. The SDKs also make sure to propagate some headers on outgoing requests so that Distributed Tracing can work effectively. For most applications, the performance overhead of enabling insights and tracing in production is imperceptible to end users. ## Will Performance break my application? Each SDK has limits on the data structures used to record all the above data. If your application is doing too many things, we will simply hit those limits and thus avoid scenarios where the SDK itself takes up too much CPU time or grows memory usage unboundedly. ### Backpressure Management Some of our backend SDKs manage backpressure internally by reducing the dynamic sampling rate when the system is in an unhealthy state. This ensures better system stability and lower SDK overhead under heavy load. The latest versions of the following SDKs support backpressure management: We will gradually roll this feature out to other backend languages in the future. ### Hosting Environment Some hosting environments have mechanisms in place that negatively influence SDK overhead: * AWS Lambdas completely freeze any code execution when a response is sent. This means that the SDKs generally will block the response from being finished until it has flushed all of the recorded telemetry data to Sentry. * SDKs that are designed to run on the Vercel Edge Runtime will stall responses to requests until the SDK has flushed all of the telemetry for that request to Sentry. This is a limitation imposed by the Edge Runtime, since it doesn't allow for I/O operations to be shared or persisted across request handler invocations, meaning the SDK cannot flush its data asynchronously.
